Exact Location: Reading: “Nutrition Affects Your Health”; Quiz Q8–15
Specific Issue: The reading uses moral/guaranteed language (“good nutrition = …”; “poor nutrition = …”), while most of the quiz tests food labels, food safety, breakfast, activity and balanced meals before those topics are taught.
Recommended Solution: Replace guaranteed language with “can support” and “patterns low in key nutrients may contribute to.” Label the quiz as a baseline pre-assessment, do not grade it, and repeat it as a post-assessment at course end.

Exact Location: Reading: fruit and dairy sections; Quiz Q10
Specific Issue: The lesson says whole fruit has “less sugar” than juice and marks fresh fruit as inherently more nutrient-dense than frozen or canned fruit. Fortified almond milk is also grouped with dairy without explaining that protein and nutrient profiles differ.
Recommended Solution: Say whole fruit generally contains more fiber and is easier to portion than juice. Teach that fresh, frozen and canned fruit can all be nutritious; compare added sugar/syrup. Prefer fortified soy milk as the closest dairy substitute and instruct students to compare labels.

Specific Issue: The lesson tells students to choose full-fat dairy with no added sugar, but the example later uses low-fat milk. The 21-meal assignment is too large for a 25–30 minute activity and may penalize students with limited food access.
Recommended Solution: Use neutral wording: choose dairy or fortified alternatives that fit individual needs; compare added sugar and saturated fat. Reduce the activity to three meals or one sample day and allow culturally familiar or school-meal examples.

Specific Issue: Simple carbohydrates are presented as “fast energy” and complex carbohydrates as “sustained energy,” while fats are labeled healthy, less healthy and unhealthy. This oversimplifies mixed foods and encourages food morality.
Recommended Solution: Explain that digestion speed depends on fiber, processing, portion and what foods are eaten together. Use “unsaturated,” “saturated” and “trans fat,” with guidance to emphasize unsaturated fats and limit trans fat.

Specific Issue: The lesson likely treats individual vitamins and minerals as producing immediate visible outcomes rather than supporting normal body functions; this can lead students to self-diagnose deficiencies.
Recommended Solution: Tie each nutrient to established functions and food sources, state that symptoms have many possible causes, and direct persistent concerns to a healthcare professional rather than using food intake as a diagnosis.

Specific Issue: Label evaluation is presented as a single-food judgment instead of considering serving size, eating occasion and overall pattern. “Low” and “high” thresholds need to use the FDA 5%/20% Daily Value rule consistently.
Recommended Solution: Teach the sequence: serving size, servings eaten, calories, nutrients to get more/less of, ingredient list, then context. Use 5% DV or less as low and 20% DV or more as high, with worked examples.

Specific Issue: A quiz answer identifies the cereal with 3 g fiber and 8 g added sugar as healthier than the cereal with 1 g fiber and 2 g added sugar. With only those facts, there is no single defensible answer.
Recommended Solution: Either provide full labels and ask students to explain the tradeoff, or change the options so one choice is clearly higher in fiber and lower in added sugar. Accept reasoned answers when tradeoffs exist.

Specific Issue: Meal planning can become a compliance exercise that assumes students control grocery purchasing, cooking and household budgets.
Recommended Solution: Frame the task as designing options rather than reporting family behavior. Include budget, school cafeteria, food access, cultural foods and no-cook alternatives. Grade reasoning, not whether the household follows the plan.

Specific Issue: Claims are discussed as if they are inherently deceptive, without distinguishing regulated claims from vague marketing language.
Recommended Solution: Separate nutrient-content claims, health claims, structure/function claims and unregulated marketing terms. Teach students to verify any front claim against serving size, Nutrition Facts and ingredients.

Specific Issue: A world-nutrition lesson can easily stereotype cultures or rank cuisines as healthy/unhealthy if it focuses on a few representative foods.
Recommended Solution: Use multiple examples within each region, acknowledge migration and household variation, and ask how different cuisines achieve balance rather than ranking cultures. Include student-selected family or community foods.

Exact Location: Reading: allergy statement; Activity; Quiz Q4 and Q6
Specific Issue: The reading says food allergies “require epinephrine,” which is too broad; not every reaction is treated the same. Diabetes guidance is generalized, and the lactose-intolerance answer implies avoiding milk entirely rather than using lactose-free or tolerated dairy.
Recommended Solution: Say epinephrine is the first-line emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis and students must follow their medical plan. Avoid prescribing disease diets; use clinician-directed plans. Include lactose-free milk/yogurt and fortified alternatives.

Specific Issue: “Even more for a child” and “blood is 80% water” are presented as fixed facts, while the reading uses advanced biochemical wording for middle school.
Recommended Solution: Use approximate ranges and age-appropriate language. Replace biochemical phrases with concrete functions such as transport, temperature control, digestion and waste removal.

Exact Location: Reading: 6–8 cups; beverage list; activity calculator
Specific Issue: A single 6–8 cup water target is treated as a universal recommendation, and coffee is listed as a recommended beverage for 11–14-year-olds. The online calculator asks minors for height, weight and gender without privacy guidance.
Recommended Solution: Use total-water ranges by age/sex from an authoritative source while emphasizing individual variation and food moisture. Do not recommend coffee to this age group. Remove personal-data calculators or use anonymous classroom examples.

Exact Location: Reading: “If you are thirsty…”; product reference
Specific Issue: “If you are thirsty, you are already dehydrated” is too absolute, and naming Cirkul is unnecessary product placement.
Recommended Solution: Say thirst is an early signal to drink, but needs vary and thirst is not a perfect measure. Replace the brand with “unsweetened or low-sugar flavor options.”

Exact Location: Reading: urine color chart; Quiz Q7 and Q10
Specific Issue: Clear urine is labeled overhydration, dark brown urine is labeled severe dehydration, and chest pain is grouped with signs to simply stop and drink. Quiz Q10 incorrectly implies the circulatory system is uniquely most affected.
Recommended Solution: Explain urine color is only a rough screening tool and can be affected by medicines, foods and illness. Dark brown urine, confusion or chest pain require immediate adult/medical help. Remove the “most affected system” question.

Specific Issue: The lesson risks treating all sports drinks, juice, milk, tea and water as universally good or bad without considering exercise duration, caffeine or portion.
Recommended Solution: Use scenario-based guidance: water for routine hydration; milk can contribute nutrients; juice in modest portions; sports drinks mainly for prolonged/intense activity or clinician guidance; avoid energy drinks.

Specific Issue: Hydration recommendations need specific heat, duration and intensity context; otherwise students may overdrink or misuse sports drinks.
Recommended Solution: Add a decision tree for normal school day, short practice, long/hot practice, illness and travel. Include coach/athletic trainer instructions and warning signs requiring adult help.

Specific Issue: Frequent urine-color tracking can become obsessive and is not reliable enough to be the “best” measure for every student.
Recommended Solution: Present thirst, access to fluids, urine frequency/color trends and symptoms as combined clues. Avoid daily scoring or public reporting of bathroom-related data.

Specific Issue: Hydration advice for kidney, heart, endocrine or other health conditions can become medical treatment guidance.
Recommended Solution: State clearly that students with fluid restrictions or medical conditions must follow their clinician and school health plan. Keep the lesson focused on why individual advice can differ, not disease-specific prescriptions.

Specific Issue: Snacking is defined as eating to “keep the body full,” foods are divided into healthy/unhealthy, and the quiz claims experts generally recommend one to three snacks daily. Snack needs are individual.
Recommended Solution: Define snacking neutrally as eating between meals for hunger, enjoyment or activity needs. Remove the universal snack-frequency rule. Have students compare strengths/tradeoffs rather than rank foods morally.

Lesson Title: Snack Nutrients and Fueling the Body
Specific Issue: Fiber is listed as one of six main nutrients instead of water, and every balanced snack is required to include carbohydrate, protein, fruit/vegetable and healthy fat—an unrealistic universal formula.
Recommended Solution: Correct the six essential nutrient categories to carbohydrates, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals and water; explain fiber is a type of carbohydrate. Teach flexible pairings, such as carbohydrate plus protein, based on hunger and timing.

Specific Issue: The fixed 100/200-calorie snack categories and universal sodium, fiber and protein targets are arbitrary and can encourage calorie fixation.
Recommended Solution: Remove “light/moderate/heavy” calorie labels. Teach serving context and compare similar products using %DV and ingredient quality. Avoid prescribing one snack target to all adolescents.

Lesson Title: Smart Swaps and Building Better Habits
Specific Issue: Several swaps are not nutritionally equivalent, nuts may have more sodium than crackers, and “hunger may actually be dehydration” can teach students to suppress hunger.
Recommended Solution: Describe swaps as options with different benefits, not automatic upgrades. Replace the hunger statement with: thirst and hunger can sometimes feel similar; respond to both by checking when you last ate and drank.

Lesson Title: The Impact of Snack Choices on the Body
Specific Issue: The lesson says sugary snacks cause brain fog and diabetes, salty/fried snacks cause inflammation and heart disease, and healthy snacks sharpen focus and prevent chronic illness. These are deterministic and stigmatizing.
Recommended Solution: Use pattern-based language: frequent high-added-sugar or high-sodium intake can contribute to risk over time; one snack does not determine health. Focus on dental health, fullness, energy availability and overall dietary pattern.

Specific Issue: Pre-practice examples include higher-fat/protein foods 30 minutes before exercise, which may cause discomfort. The activity asks for healthy vs. unhealthy lists.
Recommended Solution: Organize choices by time before activity: under 60 minutes emphasize easy-to-digest carbohydrate; 1–3 hours allow more protein/fat. Replace binary lists with “better fit / less ideal for this timing” and explain why.

Specific Issue: Statements such as “low fat means extra sugar or sodium was added” are framed as always true, and “10 companies make most snacks” is unsupported in the lesson.
Recommended Solution: Use “may” and require label verification. Cite or remove the market-concentration statement. Distinguish regulated FDA terms from vague words such as natural, wholesome or clean.

Lesson Title: Food Allergies: Safe and Inclusive Snacking
Specific Issue: Any allergy lesson must clearly distinguish intolerance, allergy and anaphylaxis and avoid asking students to investigate or handle classmates’ allergens.
Recommended Solution: Use school emergency-plan language, no food-sharing, label checking and cross-contact prevention. State that epinephrine is first-line for suspected anaphylaxis and emergency services/adults must be contacted.

Specific Issue: Habit messaging can imply students have complete control despite family schedule, finances, disability, culture and food access.
Recommended Solution: Teach cue–routine–reward and environment design while explicitly acknowledging constraints. Let students choose one realistic behavior they control.

Specific Issue: Rigid meal timing and “healthy routine” language can shame students whose schedules or hunger cues differ.
Recommended Solution: Use flexible anchors and planning options. Emphasize regular opportunities to eat, internal hunger/fullness cues and individualized routines.

Specific Issue: Skipping breakfast is linked directly to irritability, poor memory and crashes, and breakfast is presented as mandatory for everyone.
Recommended Solution: Say breakfast can support energy and concentration for many students, especially when hungry, but individual appetite and schedules vary. Offer portable and school-breakfast options without guaranteeing outcomes.

Specific Issue: Eating lunch at the same time and “chew thoroughly” are presented as health requirements, while school schedules often make this impossible.
Recommended Solution: Focus on allowing enough time to eat, including multiple food groups and preparing accessible choices. Avoid grading students on timing they cannot control.

Exact Location: Reading: dinner improves sleep; after-dinner advice
Specific Issue: The lesson says dinner nutrients improve sleep and tells students to drink water if not satisfied, which can encourage ignoring hunger.
Recommended Solution: Remove the sleep guarantee. Tell students to respond to hunger with an appropriate snack; water can accompany food but should not replace food when hungry.

Exact Location: Reading opening/table/bottom line; Quiz Q3, Q5, Q7
Specific Issue: The lesson attributes current mood and focus “literally” to today’s food, promises better grades/skin/kidney function, says breakfast skipping slows metabolism and causes weight gain, uses fear-based “fueling up or breaking down,” and includes college-level mechanisms.
Recommended Solution: Rewrite all causal claims as qualified associations; remove metabolism/weight-gain and appearance promises; use non-fear-based language. Simplify the quiz to applied high-school concepts and avoid reactive hypoglycemia, fat oxidation and gastric-emptying claims unless taught accurately.

Exact Location: Reading: simple/complex carbs and glycemic response
Specific Issue: Carbohydrates are likely divided into good/complex versus bad/simple categories, which is biologically incomplete and can stigmatize useful sport fuels.
Recommended Solution: Teach carbohydrate quality through fiber, processing, portion and timing. Explain that simple carbohydrates can be appropriate during prolonged activity and that whole grains/fruit generally add fiber and micronutrients.

Specific Issue: Protein lessons often imply more protein equals more muscle or faster recovery and may encourage supplement use or gram tracking in minors.
Recommended Solution: Center adequate total energy, training and distribution across meals. Use food-first examples, note that needs vary, and require clinician/dietitian guidance before supplements or individualized targets.

Specific Issue: The lesson risks labeling saturated fat foods as inherently bad and assigning immediate brain, skin or hormone outcomes to individual fat choices.
Recommended Solution: Teach unsaturated, saturated and trans fats accurately; focus on overall patterns and food sources. Remove appearance promises and explain that dietary fat supports absorption and energy but timing matters before exercise.

Specific Issue: Fixed macro percentages or an ideal plate may be presented as appropriate for every student and athlete.
Recommended Solution: Use acceptable ranges only as general education, not prescriptions. Build sample meals for different schedules and hunger levels and explain individual needs vary by growth, sport, access and medical needs.

Exact Location: Reading/quiz: pre-, during- and post-exercise fueling
Specific Issue: Specific sport-fueling recommendations can become individualized medical/performance advice and may overstate protein timing or carbohydrate rules.
Recommended Solution: Organize by activity duration/intensity and time available before exercise. Add hydration/heat safety and a statement that athletes with medical conditions or high training loads should follow a sports dietitian/medical team.

Specific Issue: Teaching adolescents to count macros can promote restrictive eating, body surveillance and disordered-eating behaviors, especially without a clinical need.
Recommended Solution: Rename to “Estimating and Balancing Macronutrient Sources.” Use label literacy and meal-building examples without daily targets, food logging, weighing or personal macro goals. Add eating-disorder sensitivity guidance.

Specific Issue: The lesson attributes fatigue, acne, mood, school performance and athletic outcomes directly to micronutrients, says vitamin E is dermatologist-recommended for clear skin, and contains duplicated quiz fragments.
Recommended Solution: Remove diagnostic and cosmetic promises. State deficiencies require assessment and symptoms have many causes. Correct quiz numbering/duplicate True–False remnants and use established nutrient functions only.

Exact Location: Reading: D/K2 interaction, vitamin E recovery, sun exposure
Specific Issue: The D2/K2 statement is questionable and too clinical, vitamin E is said to reduce soreness/fatigue and improve recovery, and students are encouraged toward sun exposure without sufficient skin-safety context.
Recommended Solution: Remove the D2/K2 calcium-routing claim unless a qualified dietitian supplies a strong citation. Describe vitamin E as an antioxidant nutrient without performance promises. Use safe-sun wording and clinician guidance for supplements.

Specific Issue: Water-soluble vitamins are often described as directly giving energy, preventing illness or being harmless because excess is excreted.
Recommended Solution: Clarify that B vitamins help energy metabolism but do not provide calories; vitamin C supports normal immune function but does not guarantee fewer illnesses. Include supplement upper-limit and medication-interaction cautions.

Specific Issue: The lesson may imply magnesium or potassium prevents cramps and improves athletic performance, while sodium guidance can be unsafe if generalized.
Recommended Solution: Explain exercise cramps are multifactorial. Teach food sources and normal functions without self-treating symptoms. Individual electrolyte or supplement plans should come from qualified professionals.

Specific Issue: The label is taught as a health score rather than one tool, and the lesson needs a current FDA label example and explicit serving-size context.
Recommended Solution: Use the current Nutrition Facts format. Start with serving size/servings consumed, then %DV, and compare similar foods for a stated purpose rather than declaring one food healthy.

Lesson Title: Macronutrients and Calories on the Food Label
Specific Issue: Heavy calorie and macro calculations can encourage fixation and may imply calories determine food quality.
Recommended Solution: Use a small number of functional calculations for label literacy. Pair calories with serving size, nutrients and intended use; do not require personal calorie tracking.

Specific Issue: %DV is based on a general 2,000-calorie reference and is not a personal requirement; students may mistake totals across foods as exact prescriptions.
Recommended Solution: Teach 5%/20% as comparison tools and state %DV is not individualized. Avoid having students chase 100% for every nutrient or diagnose deficiency from labels.

Specific Issue: Ingredient lists can be used to promote “clean eating” or imply unfamiliar/long names are harmful.
Recommended Solution: Teach descending weight order, allergens, added sugars and whole-grain identification. Avoid fear of chemical names, seed oils or approved additives; evaluate the whole product and eating pattern.

Specific Issue: The lesson may rely on outdated or oversimplified guidance and present national guidelines as individualized rules.
Recommended Solution: Cite the current Dietary Guidelines edition used, distinguish general population guidance from personal care, and include cultural relevance, affordability and access.

Specific Issue: Covering pregnancy, infancy, older adults and adolescence can become overly broad and medically prescriptive.
Recommended Solution: Keep the objective comparative: how needs change with growth and aging. Avoid meal plans or supplement instructions for pregnancy/infancy; direct those to clinicians.

Specific Issue: Students may be asked to estimate personal needs using weight, sex or activity formulas, creating privacy and eating-disorder concerns.
Recommended Solution: Use fictional profiles and ranges. Do not collect students’ weights, calories or body goals. Include disability, culture, food security and medical-plan considerations.

Lesson Title: Building a Balanced Plate & Meal Planning
Specific Issue: Meal planning can become rigid, expensive and culturally narrow, and may duplicate middle-school content without added rigor.
Recommended Solution: Add budget, cafeteria, convenience, cultural and performance constraints. Grade tradeoff reasoning and adaptability rather than compliance with a single plate.

Specific Issue: Marketing analysis may overstate manipulation or fail to distinguish evidence-based regulated claims from branding.
Recommended Solution: Have students identify audience, emotional appeal, influencer tactics, package design and regulated claims, then verify against label evidence and source credibility.

Specific Issue: Teaching special diets can normalize self-diagnosis, fad diets or disease treatment by students.
Recommended Solution: Differentiate medically required diets, ethical/religious patterns and trends. Do not provide treatment plans. Use clinician-directed case studies and emphasize risks of unnecessary restriction.

Specific Issue: Energy balance material can reduce health to weight change and prompt personal calorie calculations among minors.
Recommended Solution: Teach energy as supporting growth, learning, organ function and activity. Use fictional examples, avoid weight-loss assignments and include genetic, developmental and environmental complexity.

Specific Issue: The lesson may repeat Course 1 without a new learning objective and overstate which fuel is used at a given intensity.
Recommended Solution: Either merge with Course 1 or make this lesson explicitly about flexible fuel use across intensities. Avoid presenting the body as switching exclusively between carbs and fat.

Specific Issue: This substantially duplicates Course 2 and risks repeating unsupported performance/appearance claims.
Recommended Solution: Convert it into an applied synthesis lesson using food patterns and case studies, or remove it. Keep claims to established functions and avoid symptom diagnosis.

Lesson Title: Pre, During, and Post Activity Fueling
Specific Issue: Timing rules and quantities may be too prescriptive for all sports, body sizes and medical conditions.
Recommended Solution: Use broad examples based on time to activity and duration. Include gastrointestinal tolerance, heat, access and sport rules; refer individualized plans to a sports dietitian.

Specific Issue: Rigid meal frequency and timing may be presented as required and can conflict with hunger cues, culture, school schedules or medical needs.
Recommended Solution: Teach regular access to nourishment and flexible planning. Avoid claiming everyone must eat every set number of hours.

Specific Issue: The title assumes recovery problems are caused by protein and may promote overconsumption.
Recommended Solution: Rename “Protein, Total Energy and Recovery.” Explain that inadequate calories, carbohydrate, sleep, training load and injury also affect recovery.

Specific Issue: This topic is essential but high-risk; discussing RED-S, body weight or symptoms without safeguards can trigger or encourage self-diagnosis.
Recommended Solution: Use trauma-informed, non-weight-focused language. Include signs that require a trusted adult/health professional, confidentiality guidance and no personal intake/body assignments.

Specific Issue: Exact drinking schedules or sodium prescriptions can be unsafe; overhydration warning signs require medical escalation.
Recommended Solution: Teach risk factors and emergency signs, not personal prescriptions. Follow school athletic trainer/medical protocols and state confusion, vomiting, collapse or seizures require emergency response.

Specific Issue: The lesson may frame low-carb intake as always a mistake and use advanced glycogen/oxidation claims without context.
Recommended Solution: Explain that high-intensity and prolonged activity generally rely heavily on carbohydrate, but needs vary. Keep mechanisms age-appropriate and avoid diagnosing performance from one meal.

Specific Issue: Students may self-diagnose iron, vitamin D or other deficiencies from fatigue or performance and start supplements.
Recommended Solution: State symptoms are nonspecific and diagnosis requires clinical assessment/labs. Use food-first prevention, identify higher-risk groups carefully, and explicitly prohibit self-supplementation based on the lesson.
